1:
Who is told to gather is the first question, and no two answer alike. Henry lets the summons face either way, as a call to the enemies of Zion to come and do their worst, God suffering them to do it, or as a challenge to her friends to come and do their best; let them gather in troops, he says, yet it shall be to no purpose. Wesley names the addressee as one of the great northern capitals and the besieger as one of their kings. Gill argues against reading it of Jerusalem at all and prefers the Babylonians, whose armies were large, called out by the people of God to muster all their forces, since the promises assure them that in the issue they shall prevail; but he offers a second reference he plainly likes better, the Romans, to whom the character well agrees, of whose legions all have heard, and who come in naturally here because the earlier attempt on the city and the captivity have already been foretold with the deliverance from them. Calvin keeps Jerusalem as the one addressed and hears a play in the words, the verb and the noun sounding alike, as though the prophet said, thou shalt be collected, O daughter of collection. He knows the explanation that the name marks a populous state now so straitened that none dare go beyond the gates, and takes it another way: her citizens were wont to occasion great troubles, as thieves agree together and meet in troops for plunder.

The smiting of the judge is read historically by nearly all. Wesley identifies the judge as the king and warns that Israel here means not the ten tribes but the two that adhered to the house of David, adding that a rod on the cheek is a proverbial speech for the most contemptuous usage. Ellicott finds the fulfilment in the indignities that happened to the last king of Judah, and notes that the verse coheres better with the previous chapter, to which it is attached in the Hebrew. Clarke reports the same opinion from some commentators, that the chapter opens with a prophecy of the siege and of the indignities that king should suffer. Henry extends the blow to a class, the king, the chief justice and the inferior judges, used as shamefully as common captives; and he reads the disgrace as deserved, since complaint had already been made that these judges were corrupt and took bribes, so the treatment came justly for abusing their power, though it was still a calamity for the nation to see its judges so used. He reports the reading that refers the smiting to indignities done to the Messiah, and prefers the former.

Why a threat stands between two promises is Calvin’s question, answered as a matter of teaching method. It was needful to put the faithful in mind often of the approaching calamity, lest terror wholly discourage them when it came; for when the prophets threaten we either become torpid or grow angry with God and murmur, and when they set forth comfort we indulge ourselves and become too secure. It is therefore necessary to connect threatenings with promises, so that we may be ready to endure temporal evils while our minds, sustained by hope, depend on the Lord. He also answers the objection that the two pictures will not agree, the enemies trodden like sheaves and the city meanwhile besieged, by observing that the temporary punishment God inflicts on his Church does not prevent him restoring it whenever it pleases him. Henry reaches the same place from the other side: having shown how low the house of David should be brought, and how vilely the shield of that mighty family should be cast away, the prophet adds an illustrious prediction of the Messiah to encourage a people now tempted to think the covenant with that house abrogated.
2:
The double name is explained alike by all. Gill says the place is called by both its names to point it out the more distinctly, the first signifying the house of bread, a proper place for Christ to be born in who is the bread of life, and the second from its fruitfulness, as the shepherds watching their flocks near it at the birth show; the second name also distinguishes it from another town of the name in Zebulun, from which the Messiah was not to come. Clarke gives the same reason for the addition, and holds that this verse should begin the chapter, the first belonging to the one before. Wesley and Ellicott both derive the older name from the fertility of the country, Ellicott noting that the modern and the ancient names are here united. Keil and Delitzsch set the verse in the argument: the announcement of the glory Zion is to attain is completed by the birth of the great Ruler who will lead Israel to that goal, the government that returns to Zion proceeding out of little Bethlehem.

How the Gospel handles the verse is harder. Ellicott calls the passage one of immense significance through the interpretation the chief priests and scribes gave it, and treats the citation as free: they quote evidently from memory, their first variation being in the title of the town, where they give the land of Judah for the older name; the word for thousands they paraphrase by princes; and the conjunction they use shows the quotation to be a paraphrase conveying the ultimate intention of the words, which contrast the smallness of the division with the greatness of its destiny. Calvin faces the same difficulty and refuses the usual escape. Because the Gospel says the town is by no means the least, some read the prophet as a question, whether it is the least among the provinces; but that does not follow, since to say it was not the least is not to deny that it was small, and there is no contradiction in the expressions. The Evangelist, he observes, quotes literally neither the Hebrew nor the Greek, giving the sense but not the words here as in two other places, so there is no need of distorting the prophet, whose passage he meant only to point out. The two look at the town at different moments, he adds: the Gospel regards it at the coming of Christ, when it began to be eminent, while the prophet represents how mean a place it then was.

What the thousands are is settled from custom. Calvin rejects the explanation that there might be a thousand towns in the tribe among which this one could hardly find a place, as said through ignorance of a prevailing usage: the districts were divided into thousands, so that a town which with its villages could bring forth three thousand men had three prefectures, and the prophet means this town was hardly sufficient to make one. Clarke reaches the same sense by comparison, the tribes being divided into small portions called thousands as certain divisions of counties in his own country are called hundreds. On the last clause the voices converge. Clarke takes it that in every age, from the foundation of the world, there has been some manifestation of the Messiah, from the promise in paradise to the manifestation in the flesh, so that there was no time in which he has not been going forth; and as creator of all things, he argues, he is the Eternal and no part of what was created. Wesley says in a line that the generation of the Son of God, equal with his Father, is eternal. Ellicott sets the two nativities side by side, the birth of the ruler contrasted with an eternal nativity whose depth passes the comprehension of human intellect and must be spiritually discerned.
3:
Why the people should be given up is answered differently. Gill takes the giving up as the long stretch of trouble between the prophet and the birth: the siege in the days of Hezekiah, the captivity after it, the enemies who disturbed the rebuilding of the city and temple, and the tribulation of the days of the Maccabees, so that they were never long in quiet until the coming of the Messiah. Keil and Delitzsch locate the reason not in the appearance of the Ruler but in the place he springs from: because he comes from little Bethlehem, and so from a degraded branch of the family of David, his birth there rather than in the city of David presupposes that the family had already fallen. Calvin reads the verse as a deliberate moderation, preparing the godly to bear evils and not be depressed by extreme fear; two things stand together, that the people as they deserved would be heavily afflicted, and that God would still be mindful of his covenant so as to gather some remnant at last, a middle course between prosperity and destruction.

The travailing woman divides them. Calvin knows the reading that applies her to the mother of Christ and calls it forced; he takes the similitude of the body of the people instead, noting that the same figure is used elsewhere of the wicked, who promise themselves impunity and are suddenly laid hold on, whereas its force here is the opposite, the people being like a woman with child in this, that after the greatest sorrows a joyful issue follows. Clarke takes the woman for the Christian Church, represented elsewhere as a woman in travail, and reads the verse of a long postponement: the disobedient are given up into the hands of the nations until the fullness of the Gentiles is brought in, and then the remnant returns, taking in both families, so that the ten tribes, wherever they now are, shall be brought in. Ellicott hears a suggestion of parable in the smallness of the town which gave birth to the mighty Ruler; so the nation itself was to be brought very low before the nativity.

On the standing and the feeding they agree, and divide the emphasis. Gill notes only that the subject is the ruler already prophesied of, whom a Jewish commentator also interprets of the Messiah. Calvin makes the standing a matter of duration: the word designates perseverance, so the gathering of the remnant would not be for a short time, nor as it often happens when some rays of joy shine and immediately vanish, but a kingdom permanent through an unbroken series of ages. The strength he takes for power sufficient to defend a Church tossed by many tempests and never without enemies. The feeding he takes for the manner of the rule: Christ reigns not as a dreaded tyrant who distresses his subjects with fear, but as a shepherd who deals gently with his flock, and prefers that title to the name of king. Ellicott holds the two together: he shall stand with the majesty of an assured sovereignty, uniting the dignity of a king with the tenderness of a shepherd, a thought which underlies the older notion of a monarch and becomes an attribute of the King Messiah. He notes that the words his God mark a subordination to the Father, and says no event short of the foundation of the Christian faith can satisfy the prophecy. Clarke has the Messiah remaining with his followers, supporting and governing them, and reports a variant: where the text has that they shall abide, a different pointing gives that they shall be converted, the reading of three manuscripts and three ancient versions. Keil and Delitzsch add that under this rule the people attain perfect peace, the Ruler being not merely the author of peace but carrying it within himself.
5:
Two voices insist the opening clause belongs with what goes before. Clarke says it should be joined to the preceding verse, since it finishes the prophecy concerning the author of peace who shall give peace to all nations, and treats the coming of the Assyrian as a new prophecy about the subversion of that empire. Ellicott connects it the same way and presses the wording: the man is not said to bring peace but to be Peace himself, an idiom he compares with the psalm where David says he is Prayer. Gill notices the same from the Hebrew, that the word man is not in the text, only the pronoun, referring to the person already spoken of. Calvin takes peace first in the plainest sense, a quiet and peaceable inhabitation under Christ, and answers the objection that the land had been so often wasted by pointing to the King the Father has given: let his shadow suffice us and we shall be safe enough. But he refuses to stop there. Christ is our peace in another way, by reconciling us to the Father; what would it avail to be safe from earthly annoyances if we were not certain God is reconciled to us? Were all men our friends, miserable still would be our condition unless our consciences were pacified by the confidence that God is our Father.

Who the seven shepherds and eight principal men are, nobody settles. Clarke lays out three answers and chooses none: one takes them for the seven of the Maccabean family and the eight princes of the line that followed; a second treats seven and eight as a definite put for an indefinite number and understands the chiefs who took Nineveh; a third refers the whole to a later invasion, when seven magi were raised up and afterwards put to death by Persian chiefs. Wesley takes the simple course, a certain number put for an uncertain, and identifies the we of the verse as the king with the prophets and people. Ellicott admits that the invasion feared at the time does not answer the event described, suggests the Maccabean period, then offers a spiritual reading, that the passage points to the anointed men who as Christian pastors receive their commission from the Messiah. Calvin gives them a twofold office: chosen by an oppressed Church, they are to nourish it and to destroy the enemy land so that nothing remain whole, God arming them with warlike courage.

The land named beside Assyria is explained and then widened. Clarke identifies it as Assyria with its capital, and Babylon, built by the same founder; the entrances he takes for the posts or watergates, since it was by mastering the river that the Medes and Persians took the city; he refers the passage best to the invasion under Nebuchadnezzar and the destruction of that empire by Cyrus. Ellicott renders the verb literally as to feed upon, consume, depasture, and makes the land of Nimrod the opposing world-power. Wesley agrees the two names are one land, takes the entrance for the fortified frontiers, and calls the Assyrian the type of all other enemies. Calvin argues to the same generality: the two nations are named because they were then in contest with the people of God, but the prophet takes a part for the whole and means all the enemies of the Church. He ends by reminding the faithful that they needed patience, since no deliverance was to be expected until they had yielded their necks to the yoke. Gill and Keil and Delitzsch read the wasting as more than military: Gill takes the sword for the sword of the Spirit, subduing the nations to the obedience of Christ through the Gospel, and Keil and Delitzsch say the Messiah proves himself peace not only by protecting his people but by giving them power to overcome their enemies spiritually and bodily.
7:
The remnant is defined before the figure. Gill takes it of the Jews converted in the latter day, the remnant according to the election of grace, with all true Israelites whether Jews or Gentiles: a small number, mean in the eyes of men, whom God has reserved for himself, and who, though not of the world, are in it, a distinct people of no account and yet visible and wonderfully preserved. Henry adds the images: the people of God are a remnant, a small number against the many left to perish, and yet a people in covenant with God; the Church lies dispersed in the midst of many people, as gold in the ore or wheat in the heap. Israel according to the flesh dwelt alone and was not numbered among the nations, but the spiritual Israel lies scattered as seed sown in the ground, here a grain and there a grain. Calvin confines the promise for the same reason: since the prophet had spoken of destruction before, this belongs not to the whole body of the people but to the seed God preserved in the almost total ruin of the Church, and the contrast is deliberate, a remnant set among great nations.

What the dew is meant to teach divides into two answers. Calvin finds two promises in it, that God will defend his Church without the aid of men, and that he will supply it with strength enough to be superior to all its enemies; the similitude shows that the preservation of the Church depends on the mere favour of God, since he will make his people grow like grass fed only by the dew of heaven, without labour on the part of men. Wesley reads the same independence and adds the benefit: the remnant shall multiply like dew that refreshes the grass and be a blessing to those about them, God blessing them by his immediate hand, as he alone gives dew and showers without the help of man.

Henry finds six things in the comparison and counts them. The remnant is of heavenly extraction, as dew comes from the Lord, the father of the rain, so they are born from above and do not savour the things of the earth. They are numerous as the drops of dew in a summer morning. They are pure and clear, not muddy and corrupt, but crystal drops. They are produced silently, as the dew distils insensibly, which is the way of the Spirit. They live in continual dependence upon God, being no more than what his free grace makes them daily. And they are great blessings to those among whom they live, since their doctrine and example and prayers work as dew does on grass, to soften others and make them fruitful.

Where the promise has been kept two voices answer historically. Clarke reports that the people were greatly favoured under a later Persian reign, those in Persia and Chaldea being protected by two of their own, and that others refer the passage to the Maccabean age; even during the captivity, he adds, many spread the knowledge of the one true God, which may be the dew meant, and when the Messiah appeared the Gospel was preached by them. On the grass he presses both clauses: it springs up without the culture of man, even the most skilful, and the sons of men are the sons of the first transgressor, so all comes through the bounty of God, who makes his sun shine on the just and the unjust. Ellicott dates it differently, taking it of the return from captivity, when the people were to pour their influence upon the nations as God-sent showers upon the grass, and then of the dispersion of Jewish Christians after a martyrdom, by which the Lord caused the knowledge of the truth with which they were cloud-charged to descend upon many people.
8:
The second figure reverses the first. Gill notes that the same people are meant as before, compared to dew and showers because they are numerous and full of blessings, and now compared to something else entirely. Wesley reduces the point to strength and courage, which the beasts of the forest dare not oppose and cannot resist. Calvin states the promise behind it, that God will arm his people with invincible and irresistible power so that they may be superior to all their enemies: as a strong lion is superior to other beasts, and a young lion dares ferociously to attack a flock of sheep, so the people shall be, filling their enemies with terror, scattering them, so that none dare resist. Ellicott holds the two figures together as belonging to one person, since there is righteous wrath as well as all-embracing mercy with God, and the one whose graciousness is likened to the dew and whose gentleness to the lamb is at the same time the Lion of the tribe of Judah; he recalls the vision in which the kings of the earth and the great men are represented as in extreme terror at the wrath of the Lamb.

Calvin is the one voice who stops to limit the figure, and he limits it carefully. The prophet does not mean that the people of God would be cruel and sanguinary, for when the prophets use similes of this kind they express something not strictly suitable; who would be so foolish, he asks, as to select everything that belongs to a lion and apply it to the Church of God. The reason for the similitude must therefore be observed: it was to show that the faithful shall be endued with a power so superior to that of their enemies that they shall be a terror to them, and it does not follow from this that they shall be cruel. Though God recommends the spirit of meekness to his children, Calvin says, the faithful may still be a threat to their enemies; but they ought to observe what is just towards them and to keep themselves within proper bounds.

Whose hand is lifted up and when is the last question. Gill offers two answers, the hand of the church prevailing over its enemies, or the hand of the Messiah, the ruler in Israel and the man of peace who delivers, who will be at the head of his people and destroy their enemies with the sword that proceeds out of his mouth. Clarke keeps it historical throughout, supposing that this verse and the one before foretell the victories of the Maccabees, and identifying the enemies cut off as the Assyrians who destroyed the northern kingdom and the Babylonians who ruined the southern. Calvin sets the difficulty out plainly instead of solving it. The promise, he observes, is not that the Church shall be in a quiet state but that it shall be victorious, and it declares at the same time that enemies will never be wanting, so that it arms us for enduring patiently, since we cannot conquer except by fighting. Then he asks when this promise has been fulfilled, since after the exile the people were always either tributaries or kept under cruel tyranny, or at the least unequal to their enemies. His answer is that the faithful ought to be satisfied with victory itself: however hard they may be pressed, and however constant and wearisome the contests they have to carry on, this one thing ought still to be sufficient for them, that they shall not wholly perish; and it is evident that the people of God have always been preserved by his invincible hand, however numerous their opposing enemies. He adds the qualification he has kept in view throughout, that the promise is made not to the whole people but to a residue only.
10:
That the stripping is a kindness and not a punishment is agreed. Wesley says it plainly, that the cutting off is not in judgment but in mercy, since there shall be no need of these things and the church shall no more rely on them. Gill sets the day in the Gospel dispensation: they should not dwell in fortified cities and walled towns nor need them, their enemies being subdued, and the Lord himself would be their stronghold, a wall of fire round about them, so that the words express the greatest tranquillity and safety, a people living in the open, free and undisturbed. Clarke reduces it to a sentence, that they shall have no need of fortified cities because God will be their defence. Ellicott adds the legal point, that horses were imperatively forbidden to the king, though the land was described in that age as full of horses with no end to its chariots; as symbols of the power of man these are cut off, so that the reliance of the Church may be on God alone, fenced cities and the other paraphernalia of war being unnecessary in the kingdom of the Messiah. Keil and Delitzsch treat the closing summary as a rounding off, in which the only objects of idolatrous worship named are the sacred posts and the only materials of war the cities, walled and gated and bolted; these two rather subordinate objects, they say, stand for all the rest, to express the entire abolition of war.

Calvin divides the list in two and explains the halves differently. Cities, fortified places, horses and chariots are not in themselves to be condemned, since God created horses for the use of men; the fault in them is accidental, for when men abound in forces they instantly fix their hope on them, and because this people placed confidence in earthly things the salvation of God could not come to them except by stripping them of all false confidence. The groves and carved images and diviners are another matter, corruptions which closed the door against the favour of God, since a people given to idolatry could neither call upon him nor hope in him. The sum, he says, is that the Church shall not be saved by the kindness of God otherwise than by being deprived of all her own strength, and by having those obstacles removed which in a manner prevented his hand from being put forth to save.

The purpose of the stripping is then pressed home. It is not, Calvin insists, that they may be plundered with impunity, but that the favour of God may be made glorious in their deliverance; for they could not ascribe to their cities that enemies were kept off, but were constrained to acknowledge the hand of God and confess him their only deliverer, since there was no other aid for them in the land. From this he draws a rule for his own readers: the faithful have no cause to murmur if they are without great riches and not formidable for the number of their men, because it is the will of the Lord that we should be like sheep, depending wholly on his power and knowing we cannot be safe except under his protection. He observes how little even that teaches us, since destitution hardly extorts from us a real confession that our safety is in the hand of God; we are always proud. And he ends with the hardest form of the thought: if the Church were in a flourishing state with all enemies subdued and no danger, earth and heaven could not bear the foolish self-confidence of men, so there is no wonder that God holds us in, and that while he supports us by his grace he deprives us of all earthly helps, that we may learn that he alone is the author of our salvation.
12:
The two terms in the first verse are not easily distinguished, and Calvin declines to try. The prophet mentions two words meaning nearly the same thing, he says; some in that age were called augurs or diviners and others jugglers or astrologers, now called fortune-tellers, but we cannot know of a certainty what kind of superstition either was, and there is no necessity of much labour on it. What matters is the point the prophet is making, that the people could not be preserved by God unless they were cleansed from these defilements. Calvin adds the history that makes the promise necessary: these superstitions were forbidden by the Law, but the Law was not able to restrain the wickedness of that people, who continually turned aside to these evils. The reminder is therefore for their benefit, that it was through their own fault that they laboured under constant miseries and were not helped by the hand of God, since while they were full of auguries and divinations there was no room for the exercise of his favour.

The others take the promise as a clean sweep. Gill says the arts named had been practised among the Jews though forbidden them, and that nothing of the kind will be found in the Christian church of Jews and Gentiles in the latter day, when all unlawful arts and all cheating and juggling in religious matters will cease and be no more. Clarke states the positive side, that they shall seek help only in the Lord their God, and adds the historical observation that from the captivity to his own day they have had neither soothsayers, images, groves nor high places. Wesley puts the whole verse in a line, that God will in mercy to his people take away these occasions of sin.

On the images the voices divide over what the promise looks at. Gill distinguishes the two kinds, the first made of wood or stone and the second molten or cast of gold, silver or brass, and then insists on the time reference. The Jews, he says, have had no idols nor idolatrous worship since the captivity, so the prophet is not speaking of something to be found among them and removed at their conversion; he speaks of what was in his own time, or had been, and of what shall not be in the time to come when they turn to the Lord and are like dew among the people. Wesley reads the same fact the other way, as a fulfilment already given, since the people to this day hate images for divine uses and learnt that in their captivity. Clarke says only that they shall be no more an idolatrous people.

Calvin calls the verse plain and containing nothing new, and uses it for a larger point. God cannot become propitious to his Church, to keep her and make her safe, until he purges her from her filth, from idolatry and the other vices by which his worship was corrupted or even entirely subverted. From this he argues that God anticipates us by his gratuitous goodness, not only by forgiving us but by calling us back when we wander into the right way. Since we have deviated, and God withdraws his hand so that it appears he has cast us away, we ought not only to pray him to have mercy but to ascribe to him a higher favour, since he takes away the very impediments which separate us from him. God is not only inclined to pardon when men repent, Calvin says; it is his peculiar office to remove the obstacles, and this ought to be carefully noticed, that we may know our salvation proceeds from its first beginning out of the mere favour of God. He closes with the reason the images are abominated at all, that God sees his honour transferred to them.
14:
The groves are agreed to be more than trees. Gill takes them for plantations made for idolatrous worship, raised in the reigns of some of their kings contrary to the law of God, and says there should now be nothing of the kind, all idolatry being rooted out. Wesley says only that they are the groves which the people abused by idolatrous worship. Ellicott allows a wider sense, either the statues, the pillars or the trees connected with the worship of two named deities, and recalls that a statue of the kind was once placed even in the house of the Lord, from which a later king brought it out and burnt it. Calvin explains why trees should be idolatrous at all: wherever there were high and lofty trees the people thought something divine was hid under their shade, and imagined such places acquired a sort of sanctity from them, as they also thought themselves nearer to God upon a hill. He connects the verse with the one before it, as though the prophet had said that the Church could not be in safety, nor recover her pristine vigour, without being well cleansed from all the filth of idolatry.

Calvin then turns the point against reformers who did not finish. Some pious kings, when they took away the idols, did not cut down the groves, and the exception is recorded against their praise, that they worshipped God but suffered the high places to stand; the Holy Spirit does not fully commend them, because the groves were the materials of corruption, and had the people been really penitent they would have exterminated the groves by which they had so shamefully profaned the worship of God. The sum of it, on his reading, is that when God shall have well cleansed his Church and wiped away all its stains, he will then become the unfailing preserver of its safety. On the last word of the verse he reports a division: it may be rendered enemies, and many so render it, while others translate it cities. Ellicott takes the cities and reads them figuratively, as the pollutions and tumults of which the cities were the strongholds.

The vengeance at the end is read for its measure. Calvin observes that God names his wrath and his fury so that the faithful might feel greater confidence, since though their enemies poured forth grievous threatening this could not prevent God from aiding his people; if we compare the wrath and fury of God with all the terrors of men, the threats of men would appear as nothing but smoke. On the closing words he departs from the common construction. Almost all interpreters, he says, join the relative to the word for nations, so the sense is vengeance upon nations that have been rebellious against God, not hearing being to despise his power obstinately and to be moved neither by promises nor by threatenings; but a fitter sense may be elicited by referring the relative to the vengeance instead, so that God takes vengeance in a manner unheard of and incredible. By the nations, Calvin adds, the prophet understands indiscriminately all the enemies of the Church. Ellicott keeps the common construction and sharpens it, rendering the clause of nations which have not been obedient, that is, which had not availed themselves of the opportunities of learning the true religion. Wesley takes the other side, that the manner is unprecedented, and adds that the Son will be given either the hearts or the necks of his enemies, and will make them either his friends or his footstool. Clarke reads the promise as already kept, since the empires of the Assyrians and Chaldeans and the rest, the sworn enemies of that people, have long since been utterly destroyed. Gill widens it instead, taking the nations for all that are enemies to Christ and his church and people.
